episode.title: How is the death of Pierre Damas Bel resonating with Ohio’s Haitian community?
episode.description:
On Monday, Pierre Damas Bel died. His family believes he died by suicide, motivated by the loss of his temporary protected status -- a loss that many Haitian immigrants experienced earlier this summer.

As a result, President Trump’s immigration policies have become a flashpoint in Bel's death. How is it resonating with the Haitian community in Springfield, Ohio?


This episode was produced by Erika Ryan and Karen Zamora, with audio engineering by Becky Brown, Éowyn Fain and Ted Mebane. 

Our director is Jonas Adams.

It was edited by Sarah Handel and Tinbete Ermyas.

Our interim executive producer is Courtney Dorning.

utterances.speaker: A
utterances.text: Can you just first tell me a little bit about Pierre? What was he like?

utterances.speaker: D
utterances.text: Pierre was friendly, joyful. Everyone who knew him loved him. His teachers speak well of him. He works at the Texas Roadhouse. His fellow Employees and managers speak well of him. He was just a joyful, very smart young man who wanted to be a doctor.

utterances.speaker: A

utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, they're devastated, like, you know, all of our families would be. I think the difference is they're devastated and they're angry because This was just so unnecessary. This young man had never even had a traffic ticket, posed no threat at all. He was just terrified of going back to Haiti.

utterances.speaker: A
utterances.text: Yeah. What is Pierre's family saying to you about his death? Why do they think it happened?

utterances.speaker: D
utterances.text: They believe that it happened because of the ankle monitor. He was teased at school about it. He's a student at Wright State. He posted about it. He talked with friends about it. I mean, there are two things. He was ashamed of it and he was afraid of going back to Haiti. So it's a combination of those, those two things. And I think what, what kind of pushed him over the brink was in the ROTC class, they were handing out uniforms and everyone in the class got a uniform except for him. And he was told he couldn't get one because of the his immigration status or the ankle monitor.

utterances.speaker: A
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. This is so horrific. And I'm wondering if you've had a sense to talk to a number of people in the Haitian community in Springfield, and if you're gathering just how this death this week is affecting the broader community there, the broader Haitian community.

utterances.speaker: D
utterances.text: Well, I've heard lots of reports of people who are suicidal. So in some sense, this doesn't come as a as a big surprise. It's like every time the Haitian community begins to get their balance, they get hit again. And they've taken one hit after another here in Springville. The first one recently was when they started getting letters telling them they had to show up at the ICE office down in Blue Ash or over in Westerville. And that's where they get the ankle monitors, which everyone here refers to as shackles now. Then the second blow was there's There's just a dramatic increase in ICE activity. They're here every single day picking up people. They seem to want to do it in areas where lots of people see them. It's usually on the main, one of the main streets, gas stations or grocery stores. They are just terrified. And it's hard because they've all lost their jobs. They don't have money. People are trying to take food to them. And they're just, they're afraid to come out of their homes, but they are more afraid of going back to Haiti.

I was walking into an ICE appointment with a man from my church, and as we were walking down the sidewalk to the door, he leaned over and he said, "Pastor, the gangs in Haiti just kidnapped my brother." And I said, "What happened to him?" And he said, "They burned him." I said, "Is he okay?" And he said, "No, they burned him alive." And I've heard multiple stories like that just from the small sample of Haitians who attend my church. You know, I talked to a reporter who's down there right now. He's embedded with the gang suppression regiment. And he said people who've been deported are getting off the planes and running for their lives. You know, part of what happens, the government talks about giving them $2,400 or $2,600 if they self-deport. The gangs assume everyone's getting off the plane has that money. So they are targets and they don't have that. I haven't heard of anyone getting that money. I've heard they get $65 from someone in Haiti and that's it. So the level of fear is just so, so high, they will do anything, including take their lives, not to go back.
